horoscopes.intro: November 18 in the stars: Find out what’s in store for you today in our daily horoscopes for Wednesday November 18. Read the daily horoscopes for your Sun sign or rising sign (ascendant) to plan your day.

aries.text: From your wardrobe to your voting record, today’s dynamic duet of the Sun and Jupiter wants a statement from you. People have always looked to you as proof that living out loud is survivable, even if you’ve been watering down your sharper opinions lately to keep the peace. Enough of that. Today your uncensored nerve is the thing others find contagious, whether you’re posting about a policy you can’t stomach or telling the object of your affections exactly how interested you are.

taurus.text: You’d hate to let a friend down or skip a good happy hour, Taurus. Some days, though, the pressure to keep up appearances should not be succumbed to. As vivacious Jupiter squares the Sun, you may be running low or feeling introspective, so don’t fight it. If you want the sound of another human, put on a podcast while you cook something healthy for dinner. One more thing: let the calls from your most demanding relatives go to voicemail. They’ll have to manage without the family rock for one evening.

gemini.text: You won’t have to go looking for things to criticize today, Gemini, because alas, they’ll present themselves in a glaring fashion. Thanks to an agitating Sun-Jupiter square, other people’s harmless little habits can really get under your skin. Breathe. Then take yourself out of range with a long walk or a vigorous workout, anything that puts distance between you and the nearest tapping pen. If you’ve been squabbling with a good friend, or can feel a row brewing, tell them you’re taking the day for yourself and you’ll circle back tomorrow.

cancer.text: Everything shiny will look like a necessity today, Cancer, but that doesn’t mean you should add it to a cart. With a decadent Sun-Jupiter mashup overhead, retail therapy has unusually strong pull. If you’re saving for something big, stay off the luxury sites “just to look,” because your restraint isn’t at full strength. That said, don’t deny yourself aesthetic pleasure altogether. Catch an exhibit after work, put on a film with gorgeous cinematography, or get outside while the last leaves are still hanging on. You may come home wanting to create some art yourself.

leo.text: Familiarity can breed contempt as Jupiter in your sign catches fire from the Scorpio Sun. Yesterday, it was nothing but warmth with your chosen family and closest relatives. Today, even their sweetest habits will scrape against your nerves like sandpaper. At moments like this, your smartest play is to make a little distance, even if that means popping on headphones or taking a short drive around town. Better that than to snap at them over a harmless “slip” or, worse, for merely occupying the same room.

virgo.text: Your heart—and the rest of you—could use a reprieve from playing caretaker to everyone in your orbit. Can you claim a personal day for yourself? And if you ARE at home, grab the softest blanket in the house and build yourself a nest as your “office.” Whatever your off-hours happen to be, do what you can to make them more restorative. Invest in a proper teapot for steeping loose-leaf or a pair of noise-canceling headphones for playing something meditative…and tuning out relatives and roommates when you need a minute.

libra.text: Shake up your routines under today’s galvanizing Sun-Jupiter square—yes, even if they’re already in complete disarray. This biannual mashup calls for spontaneity and adventure, and you’ll have to scrounge it up any way you can. Locate the slack in your schedule and let your whims take the wheel for an hour or so. This could send you down a craft rabbit hole or on a recipe reconnaissance mission. And hey, the morning meeting doesn’t need to know you were chopping vegetables for a pot of soup the whole time, right?

scorpio.text: Keep a major goal in your sight—and don’t let anything pull focus—as the Scorpio Sun and lucky Jupiter compose a dynamic duet in the most ambitious parts of your chart. But that doesn’t mean toeing a narrow line today. Figure out ways to marry your social appetites with your career aspirations. If springing for the ticket to a charity gala means “mingling” with the people YOU regard as influential, consider it an investment in your future. And if you need a couple of hours to build out one of your bigger ideas, move an appointment and hunker down until it’s real.

sagittarius.text: No matter how “enchanted” something looks or feels, keep at least one eyebrow raised today. With the Sun and your rose-tinted ruler Jupiter lowering your guard, you could fall under the spell of a persuasive operator. If an offer seems too good to be true, well, you know how this goes—it probably is. And if people rush you to sign on any dotted lines or produce a deposit, invent a reason to slip away—and feel no obligation to return. It’s far harder to climb out of situations like these than it is to tumble into them.

capricorn.text: Keeping secrets won’t be simple under today’s loose-lipped Sun-Jupiter square, but do your best to seal confidential material in the vault. Even if you’re passing along stories out of concern, your blurts could circle back to haunt you. Be choosy about who you take into your confidence, and instead of getting swept into other people’s dramas, widen your world with something cultural. Stream a subtitled film or drop into a sound bath tonight.

aquarius.text: YOU know that you’ve got what it takes to steer a project, but is anyone else clued in to your talents? Don’t let your brilliance go on living as a “secret weapon,” Aquarius. Under today’s galvanizing Sun-Jupiter mashup, hunt down opportunities to elevate your professional standing. It’s not rude to ask someone “Could I send you a proposal?” (Okay, maybe save it for the third or fourth question rather than your opening line.) Don’t be shy about promoting yourself, and dress the part if you’ll be on camera! Your stylish sign knows how powerful aesthetics can be.

pisces.text: No matter how bitter the morning air might be, a 20-minute walk could be the wakeup call you need. With the Sun getting a nudge from nomadic Jupiter, this is the ideal day to take in some fresh air and enjoy the pleasure of being in motion. When you get a moment to pause, step out of the office for an unhurried stroll. Weather not cooperating? Reserve your spot in a fitness class or see if friends want to go dance to live music tonight. items.title: A genetically encoded local learning rule enables physical learning in engineered bacteria
items.originalTitle: A genetically encoded local learning rule enables physical learning in engineered bacteria
items.summary: Training physical neural networks directly in matter remains difficult because most platforms do not store and update weights within the same physical substrate. Here we show that engineered Escherichia coli can implement a genetically encoded local learning rule acting on persistent biological memory.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Training physical neural networks directly in matter remains difficult because most platforms do not store and update weights within the same physical substrate. Here we show that engineered Escherichia coli can implement a genetically encoded local learning rule acting on persistent biological memory. We introduce memregulons: bacterial memory elements in which coupled plasmids store an analogue weight as the relative abundance of P1 within the P1 + P2 plasmid pool. Environmental inputs activate local promoters, and a shared sublethal kanamycin signal converts promoter activity into differential growth that lowers the stored P1 fraction. Across single-strain trajectories, combined plate-reader and flow-cytometry measurements are consistent with activity- and variance-dependent weight change. At the single-cell level, repeated negative learning reshapes the stored weight distribution as it approaches the lower boundary. In mixed populations and co-cultures, one shared negative learning signal selectively rewrites active memregulons, enabling externally routed supervised tic-tac-toe lessons. We then generalise the architecture across orthogonal chemical inputs and combinatorial promoters, and combine measured co-culture updates with external game analysis and simulate negative pruning in nonlinear-classifier architectures. These results establish physical learning in living matter through local negative updates of genetically encoded analogue weights.

items.title: Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 participates in the internalization of arginine-rich dipeptide repeat proteins
items.originalTitle: Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 participates in the internalization of arginine-rich dipeptide repeat proteins
items.summary: Microsatellite repeat expansion of the 5' GGGGCC 3' sequence in the C9orf72 gene is the most common monogenic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia. Dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) translated from the mutant allele can be detected in postmortem brains of afflicted individuals.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
items.abstract: Microsatellite repeat expansion of the 5' GGGGCC 3' sequence in the C9orf72 gene is the most common monogenic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia. Dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) translated from the mutant allele can be detected in postmortem brains of afflicted individuals. The arginine containing peptides, poly proline-arginine (poly-PR) and poly glycine-arginine (poly-GR), are particularly noxious to cells. Both can undergo cell-to-cell transmission, but underlying mechanisms are not understood. We found rapid internalization and nucleolar localization of bath-applied hemagglutinin (HA) tagged poly-PR with twenty repeats (HA-PR20) in cell lines and neurons. Small molecule and RNAi approaches implicated a temperature-dependent, fluid phase endocytosis mechanism for HA-PR20. We sought to identify DPR-related cell surface uptake factors using µMap high-resolution proximity labeling. DPR-iridium conjugates identified candidate cell-surface proteins which were interrogated in a secondary RNAi screen. Focusing on our strongest candidate, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 (CSPG4), we showed cellular uptake of HA-PR20 is reduced by inhibition of glycosaminoglycan chain synthesis and knockdown or ablation of CSPG4. Knockdown of CSPG4 protected PR20-induced neuronal toxicity. Using a dual reporter system to interrogate in vitro neuron-to-neuron transmission of PR50, we found PR50 synthesized by one neuron readily spread to neighboring cells. Transmission was significantly reduced with CSPG4 knockdown. Similarly conditioned media from PR50 or GR50 expressing neurons contained transmissible protein that was internalized into neurons in a CSPG4-dependent manner. These results suggest CSPG4 participates in poly-PR/poly-GR internalization and transmission.

items.title: Working memory capacity moderates stress-related drinking in alcohol use disorder: An intensive one-year ecological assessment study
items.originalTitle: Working memory capacity moderates stress-related drinking in alcohol use disorder: An intensive one-year ecological assessment study
items.summary: Stress is a trigger for alcohol consumption, with working memory capacity (WMC) proposed as a protective factor.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract:
Background: Stress is a trigger for alcohol consumption, with working memory capacity (WMC) proposed as a protective factor. While several laboratory-based and cross-sectional studies point toward an interaction between WMC, stress, and alcohol consumption, ecological momentary assessments (EMAs) are needed to establish this relationship in real-life contexts, where alcohol consumption and stress experiences actually take place.

Methods: In this one-year longitudinal EMA study, we collected data from a gamified, smartphone-based WMC task (every 4 weeks) and EMAs of stress and alcohol consumption (every two days) from n=603 participants diagnosed with alcohol use disorder (AUD). We then integrated this data with structural brain imaging data to explore the neural correlates of the hypothesized moderating effect of WMC.

Results: As preregistered, we found that WMC moderated the within-subject association between stress and alcohol consumption. Participants with low WMC, but not participants with high WMC, consumed more alcohol in more stressful compared to less stressful months. In further analysis, within-subject fluctuations in WMC also moderated the within-subject association between stress and drinking. Although effects were in the expected direction, the moderating effect of WMC was not mediated by neural correlates of interest (dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and insula).

Conclusions: We provide first real-life evidence that greater WMC might increase resilience to stress-related drinking in individuals with AUD. This advances our neurocognitive understanding of individual susceptibility to stress-related drinking, which could inform the development of future, personalized interventions.

items.title: Genetically Predicted MRI Phenotypes Are Associated with Risk of Multiple Sclerosis
items.originalTitle: Genetically Predicted MRI Phenotypes Are Associated with Risk of Multiple Sclerosis
items.summary: Brain atrophy is a hallmark of multiple sclerosis (MS) and precedes clinical symptom onset. However, whether brain development and morphological measures contribute to MS susceptibility remains unclear. We investigated whether genetically determined brain imaging phenotypes are associated with MS risk.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract:
Objective: Brain atrophy is a hallmark of multiple sclerosis (MS) and precedes clinical symptom onset. However, whether brain development and morphological measures contribute to MS susceptibility remains unclear. We investigated whether genetically determined brain imaging phenotypes are associated with MS risk.

Methods: We applied causal inference approaches using genome-wide association study (GWAS) data for 170 heritable magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived phenotypes from 39,691 United Kingdom (UK) Biobank participants and leveraged with MS susceptibility GWAS data from 14,802 MS patient and 26,703 controls. Generalized summary-data-based Mendelian randomization with HEIDI filtering was used to assess putative causal associations while accounting for horizontal pleiotropy, with orthogonal sensitivity analysis using 2-sample Mendelian randomization. Significant loci underwent functional annotation, Bayesian colocalization with brain expression quantitative trait loci, integration with single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from MS postmortem tissue, and druggability assessment. False discovery rate adjustments were applied.

Results: Four MRI phenotypes were associated with MS susceptibility: cerebellar vermis VIIIa gray-matter volume, mean diffusivity of the right anterior corona radiata, intracellular volume fraction of the corpus callosum, and orientation dispersion index of the right external capsule. Functional analyses identified 120 candidate genes, including several within the complex 17q21.31 locus. Cell-type-specific Mendelian randomization identified higher genetically predicted PLEC expression in inhibitory neurons and microglia as associated with lower MS susceptibility. Differential gene expression analyses highlighted convergent dysregulation of MAPT, EGFR, and HBEGF, implicating neurodevelopmental, neurovascular, and autophagy-related pathways. Twenty-five candidate genes were identified as potentially druggable targets.

Interpretation: Genetically determined brain structural traits are associated with MS susceptibility, supporting the concept that premorbid brain architecture contributes to disease vulnerability and highlighting potential therapeutic targets. ANN NEUROL 2026.

items.title: Universal digital mental health interventions for children and youth a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.originalTitle: Universal digital mental health interventions for children and youth a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Children and youth face rising mental health challenges in an increasingly digital world. Universal Tier 1 digital mental health interventions (DMHIs)-low-intensity, high-reach supports for non-clinical populations-have emerged as scalable tools for early-stage needs, but effectiveness remains unclear.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract: Children and youth face rising mental health challenges in an increasingly digital world. Universal Tier 1 digital mental health interventions (DMHIs)-low-intensity, high-reach supports for non-clinical populations-have emerged as scalable tools for early-stage needs, but effectiveness remains unclear. This systematic review and meta-analysis of 57 studies (N = 43,973) assessed impacts across emotional, behavioural, social, and cognitive outcomes, and examined whether delivery format (hybrid vs. virtual) and timing (post-intervention vs. follow-up) influenced results. Across outcomes, 9/16 pooled effect sizes were statistically significant, indicating small effects. Hybrid interventions, those incorporating any in-person component, showed more consistent and sustained benefits, with moderate-certainty evidence at follow-up, though most pooled findings were low certainty. Parents of younger children and marginalized children and youth were notably understudied. Future research must prioritize marginalized populations, broaden outcome evaluation, and deliver large-scale, high-quality trials to inform inclusive, sustainable implementation of digital mental health supports.INPLASY registration number: INPLASY202490026.

items.title: Design Strategies in Discrete Choice Experiments for Individuals with Cognitive Impairment: A Systematic Review
items.originalTitle: Design Strategies in Discrete Choice Experiments for Individuals with Cognitive Impairment: A Systematic Review
items.summary: Patient preference evidence is increasingly important for value assessment and decision making in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). Discrete choice experiments (DCEs) are widely used to elicit patient preferences but may raise feasibility concerns in individuals with cognitive impairment.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract:
Objectives: Patient preference evidence is increasingly important for value assessment and decision making in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). Discrete choice experiments (DCEs) are widely used to elicit patient preferences but may raise feasibility concerns in individuals with cognitive impairment. We aimed to systematically review studies that explicitly evaluated design choices in DCEs for preference elicitation in individuals with cognitive impairment.

Methods: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL/PsycINFO through January 23, 2026 for studies that evaluated DCE design adaptations or feasibility in cognitively impaired populations. Findings were synthesized narratively according to adaptations and their reported effects on comprehension, task performance, and respondent burden.

Results: We identified six studies. Four categories of design adaptations were identified: attribute description, simplification of choice task structure, visual design and layout, and survey administration. We learned that attribute familiarity and concreteness improved understanding; respondents struggled when the status-quo state was not anchored to their own current health state. Limiting to three options per task and three attributes per option improved completion rates. Greater overlap in attribute levels across options made tasks easier to complete. Use of icons as illustrations improved attribute comprehension, and caregiver involvement in interviewer-administered surveys aided completion.

Conclusions: Existing evidence suggests that DCEs can be successfully completed by individuals with mild cognitive impairment or early-stage dementia when tasks are appropriately adapted to lessen complexity. However, the evidence base remains limited. Additional methodological research is needed to identify design strategies that improve accessibility of these tasks to those with cognitive challenges while generating meaningful preference information.

items.title: Educational resources for traumatic brain injury misconceptions: what works best?
items.originalTitle: Educational resources for traumatic brain injury misconceptions: what works best?
items.summary: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) misconceptions are widely held and negatively impact people with TBI. A proposed remedy is education; however, the best method is debated.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.source: Brain impairment : a multidisciplinary journal of the Australian Society for the Study of Brain Impairment
items.abstract:
Background: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) misconceptions are widely held and negatively impact people with TBI. A proposed remedy is education; however, the best method is debated.

Methods: A total of 119 adults were randomly allocated to one of three education groups: TBI facts (n = 30), TBI story (n = 45) or non-TBI information (n = 44). Participants completed a version of the Common Misconceptions About Traumatic Brain Injury Scale (CM-TBI) on two occasions, before and after education. A total score and subscale scores were analysed.

Results: Preliminary tests found no group differences due to sample demographics, such as age. A 2 × 3 mixed-design ANOVA found no significant group × occasion interaction on TBI misconceptions (total score). There were no significant main effects for occasion (P > 0.05) or group (P > 0.05). Analysis with subscale scores followed the same pattern.

Conclusion: Contrary to predictions, this study did not find that TBI information reduced TBI misconceptions. Further studies are needed to understand whether TBI information can improve misconceptions in other samples (e.g. less-educated), or with a higher information 'dose' (longer or face-to-face exposure methods). The possibility that previously reported gains might not be clinically meaningful is explored, and new research and educational directions are proposed.

items.title: Greenspace exposure and associated health outcomes: an updated systematic review of reviews
items.originalTitle: Greenspace exposure and associated health outcomes: an updated systematic review of reviews
items.summary: Studies, including umbrella reviews, have provided evidence linking greenspace exposure to specific health outcomes.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract:
Background: Studies, including umbrella reviews, have provided evidence linking greenspace exposure to specific health outcomes. To address methodological limitations in existing umbrella reviews, this umbrella review aims to expand knowledge on the association between greenspace and human health by summarising evidence from both quantitative and qualitative systematic reviews and meta-analyses.

Methods: This umbrella review builds upon our previous review with updates to reflect recent developments in the field. Five databases (PubMed, Embase, the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature [CINAHL], Scopus, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews) were searched for articles published in English in peer-reviewed journals between December 2020 and June 2024. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses were included if they clearly defined measures of greenspace exposure and reported health outcomes directly attributable to greenspace exposure (PROSPERO: CRD42022383421). The methodological quality and risk of bias of each included review were evaluated by two independent reviewers.

Results: A total of 45 articles were included in this umbrella review. Greenspace exposure was beneficially associated with mental health, general health and quality of life, and cardiovascular and metabolic health. Inconsistent or inconclusive associations were observed for respiratory health and allergies, maternal health and birth outcomes, cancer, and cognitive function. Some harmful associations were reported for communicable and vector-borne diseases, although these were based on a limited number of systematic reviews. Most of the included reviews had a high risk of bias and critically low methodological quality.

Discussion: This umbrella review highlights the multifaceted health benefits of greenspace exposure while underlining existing evidence gaps and methodological challenges. The results indicate that increasing access to greenspace could be a simple and cost-effective strategy to improve population health and reduce health inequalities.

items.title: A Systematic Review on the Impact of Mental Health on Reproductive Hormones and Fertility Outcomes
items.originalTitle: A Systematic Review on the Impact of Mental Health on Reproductive Hormones and Fertility Outcomes
items.summary: Psychological stress and mental health disorders may interact with reproductive function through neuroendocrine, metabolic, behavioural, and oxidative pathways.

items.abstract: Psychological stress and mental health disorders may interact with reproductive function through neuroendocrine, metabolic, behavioural, and oxidative pathways. This systematic review aimed to synthesize the available evidence on the relationship between psychological stress, mental health, reproductive hormones, and fertility outcomes in women and men, including outcomes associated with assisted reproductive technology (ART). PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar were searched for English-language human literature published between 2015 and 2025. Of 3,265 records identified, 1,020 duplicates were removed, 2,245 records underwent title and abstract screening, and 595 full-text reports were assessed for eligibility. Fifteen publications were included in the final narrative synthesis. The included evidence was heterogeneous and consisted predominantly of narrative reviews, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and one review of systematic reviews. A post hoc methodological appraisal was performed using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tools appropriate to the type of review. Stress-related activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis was associated across the reviewed literature with alterations in hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal signalling, with cortisol, prolactin, ghrelin, gonadotropins, and gonadal steroids implicated in proposed mechanisms. In women, the literature described associations with menstrual and ovulatory dysfunction, while male reproductive literature reported possible effects on testosterone and semen parameters. Evidence regarding a direct adverse effect of psychological distress on ART pregnancy outcomes was inconsistent, and meta-analytic evidence did not consistently demonstrate an association between pretreatment or treatment-related emotional distress and pregnancy outcomes. Psychological interventions showed more consistent benefits for reducing distress and improving coping than for improving reproductive endpoints. Psychological stress and reproductive health appear to be interrelated; however, the available evidence does not establish a definitive causal relationship between stress and impaired fertility. items.title: Sustainability of Treatment Success 5 Years after Exposure-Based Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy for Anxiety Disorders
items.originalTitle: Sustainability of Treatment Success 5 Years after Exposure-Based Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy for Anxiety Disorders
items.summary: Achieving sustainable success in the treatment of anxiety disorders remains a central objective in mental health care. Although research has demonstrated the short-term efficacy of psychotherapy, evidence regarding long-term sustainability is limited.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract:
Introduction: Achieving sustainable success in the treatment of anxiety disorders remains a central objective in mental health care. Although research has demonstrated the short-term efficacy of psychotherapy, evidence regarding long-term sustainability is limited. This study examined treatment outcomes 5 years after prediction-error-based exposure therapy.

Methods: For 355 patients (616 eligible; 58% follow-up rate), newly collected follow-up data on anxiety symptoms and psychosocial functioning were compared to pretreatment, posttreatment, and 6-month follow-up data from a multicenter clinical trial characterized by high treatment fidelity.

Results: Improvements in anxiety symptoms and psychosocial functioning that were evident at posttreatment and 6-month follow-up were largely preserved after 5 years. No significant differences emerged between randomized groups of temporally intensified and non-intensified exposure. From 6 months to 5 years, overall remission rates remained stable, with the majority of patients exhibiting no reliable change in symptom severity. Reliable relapse occurred in 4.9% and reliable new remission in 6.5%. Most patients (63.4%) did not seek additional treatment. Among those who did, depression (64.2%) and anxiety (60.5%) were the most frequently cited reasons, although only a minority (6.0%) sought further treatment exclusively for anxiety. Additional treatment during the follow-up period was associated with higher symptom severity throughout assessments.

Conclusion: These findings highlight the sustainability and long-term public health benefits of exposure-based CBT for anxiety disorders. Most patients do not need additional treatments for mental disorders even 5 years after treatment. Nevertheless, further efforts are needed to optimize interventions for those patients who do not achieve remission or experience relapse.
